title: Null-safe values in Kotlin
summary: Use immutable and mutable values, a nullable type, and a loop to count positives.

scenario.briefing: A campus dashboard summarizes stock changes and must handle missing values without crashing.

objectives.description: Apply the taught syntax in a working file.
Count positives in a new list with a standard operator.

hints: The loop already visits each value.
Increment the mutable count in the branch.

misconceptions.description: Counting zero as a positive change.
misconceptions.testDescription: The loop counts only positive values.
misconceptions.feedback: Zero is neither positive nor negative. The comparison must be value > 0, not value >= 0.

misconceptions.description: Declaring the counter with val and trying to increment it.
misconceptions.diagnostic: Declaring count with val, then assigning count += 1 inside the loop.
misconceptions.feedback: val prevents reassignment. A counter that changes needs var, while fixed inputs can stay val.

misconceptions.description: Expecting the Elvis operator to throw on null.
misconceptions.feedback: The Elvis operator supplies the fallback on the right when the left side is null. It does not throw.

misconceptions.description: Counting every element instead of only positives.
misconceptions.feedback: The list size includes zero and negative values. A predicate counts only the values that satisfy it.

sections.title: Kotlin values and decisions
sections.body: Kotlin declares immutable values with val count = 3 and mutable values with var total = 0. Type inference keeps declarations short. A nullable type is written String?. Safe calls (?.), Elvis (?:), and smart casts replace most explicit null checks. if is an expression, and when selects among several branches without fall-through. A for loop visits a range or collection: for (value in values) { ... }.

steps.title: Count positives with an operator
steps.prompt: Given val values = listOf(4, 0, -3, 7), what does values.count { it > 0 } return?
hints: The predicate runs once per element.
Negative values do not satisfy it either.

quiz.prompt: Given val values = listOf(4, 0, -3, 7), what does values.count { it > 0 } return?

options.label: 4, because count uses the list size
0, because count needs an initial value

quiz.explanation: count with a predicate increments only for elements that satisfy it. The values 4 and 7 qualify, while 0 and -3 do not.
